SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT — COURT-AUTHORIZED ESTATE PLANNING FOR A CONSERVATEE (PROB. CODE §§ 2580-2586; PROB. CODE § 6100; CONSERVATORSHIP OF HART; MURPHY V. MURPHY) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Marguerite A. Devlin · Theodore Devlin

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes what California law provides about substituted judgment — the court proceeding in which a probate court authorizes or requires a conservator of the estate to take an estate-planning or property-disposition action on behalf of a conservatee: who may file the petition and for what purposes; the fourteen kinds of action the statute lists, including gifts, the creation of trusts, changes to beneficiary designations, the making of a will, and the making or revocation of a revocable transfer on death deed; the limit the statute places on revoking or modifying a revocable trust; who must be given notice; the two determinations the court must make before it may make an order; the thirteen circumstances the court must take into consideration; what the court may do after the hearing; the standard the published decisions apply to the decision itself; the court's power to call in the conservatee's estate-planning documents; the absence of any duty on the conservator to propose such an action; the appealability of the order and the effect of an appeal; and what a substituted judgment order was held to decide for later litigation. It is prepared as background in connection with the conservatorship of Marguerite A. Devlin, the administration of that conservatorship estate by Theodore Devlin, and any proceeding concerning it in Santa Clara County, California. It states what the statutes and the published opinions say. It does not state whether any action should be proposed, whether any court would authorize it, or what any person should do.

WHAT SUBSTITUTED JUDGMENT IS (PROB. CODE § 2580(A); CONSERVATORSHIP OF HART; MURPHY V. MURPHY)
Article 10 of Chapter 6 of Part 4 of Division 4 of the Probate Code, sections 2580 through 2586, is titled "Substituted Judgment." Section 2580(a) allows the conservator or any other interested person to file a petition asking the court to authorize or require the conservator to take a proposed action, and it names three purposes for which such a petition may be filed: benefiting the conservatee or the estate; minimizing current or prospective taxes or expenses of administration of the conservatorship estate or of the estate upon the conservatee's death; and providing gifts of the kinds, and to the sorts of donees, that would be likely beneficiaries of gifts from the conservatee. In Conservatorship of Hart the Court of Appeal described the article as permitting the court to substitute its judgment for the conservatee's, and in Murphy v. Murphy the Court of Appeal described sections 2580 and following as codifying a common law doctrine and described the probate court's power under it. The article speaks throughout of a conservator and a conservatee. Whether any particular action concerning the estate of Marguerite A. Devlin falls within it is a question this sheet does not answer.

THE ACTIONS THE STATUTE LISTS (PROB. CODE § 2580(B))
Section 2580(b) says the action proposed in the petition "may include, but is not limited to," fourteen kinds of action. They are: making gifts of principal or income, or both, outright or in trust; conveying or releasing the conservatee's contingent and expectant interests in property, including marital property rights and any right of survivorship incident to joint tenancy or tenancy by the entirety; exercising or releasing the conservatee's powers as donee of a power of appointment; entering into contracts; creating revocable or irrevocable trusts of estate property for the conservatee or others; transferring to a trust created by the conservator or conservatee property unintentionally omitted from the trust; exercising the conservatee's options to purchase or exchange securities or other property; exercising the conservatee's rights under life insurance, annuities, dividend investment plans, and retirement, profit sharing and employee welfare plans, including the right to change beneficiaries or ownership; electing to take under or against a will; disclaiming an interest; revoking or modifying a revocable trust or surrendering that right; making an election referred to in section 13502 or an election and agreement referred to in section 13503; making a will; and making or revoking a revocable transfer on death deed. The list is expressly not exclusive. Which, if any, of these actions is at issue in the conservatorship of Marguerite A. Devlin is a question this sheet does not answer.

CREATING A TRUST, AND TRANSFERRING OMITTED PROPERTY INTO AN EXISTING ONE (PROB. CODE § 2580(B)(5)-(6))
Two of the listed actions concern trusts. Paragraph (5) allows the proposed action to be the creation, for the benefit of the conservatee or of others, of revocable or irrevocable trusts of the property of the estate, and it says in terms that such trusts "may extend beyond the conservatee's disability or life." The same paragraph carves out one kind of trust: a special needs trust for money paid pursuant to a compromise or judgment for a conservatee may be established only under Chapter 4 (commencing with section 3600) of Part 8, and not under the substituted judgment article. Paragraph (6) allows the proposed action to be the transfer, to a trust created by the conservator or the conservatee, of property unintentionally omitted from that trust. In Murphy v. Murphy the probate court had made an order under this article authorizing a conservator to execute a living trust and a pour-over will for the conservatee, and the Court of Appeal described the discretion and authority conferred by the article as including the creation of trusts and the making of wills. Whether any trust or transfer is proposed in the conservatorship of Marguerite A. Devlin is a question this sheet does not answer.

THE LIMIT ON REVOKING OR MODIFYING THE CONSERVATEE'S REVOCABLE TRUST (PROB. CODE § 2580(B)(11))
Paragraph (11) of section 2580(b) allows the proposed action to be the exercise of the conservatee's right to revoke or modify a revocable trust, or the surrender of that right — but it attaches a limit that appears nowhere else in the list. The court "shall not" authorize or require the conservator to exercise the right to revoke or modify a revocable trust in three situations: where the instrument governing the trust evidences an intent to reserve the right of revocation or modification exclusively to the conservatee; where the instrument provides expressly that a conservator may not revoke or modify the trust; or where the instrument otherwise evidences an intent that would be inconsistent with authorizing or requiring the conservator to exercise that right. The limit turns on the language of the particular trust instrument, and the paragraph supplies no standard for reading that language beyond the words quoted below. What any trust instrument of Marguerite A. Devlin provides, and whether it falls within any of these three situations, are questions this sheet does not answer.

MAKING A WILL FOR THE CONSERVATEE (PROB. CODE §§ 2580(B)(13), 6100)
Two sections of the Probate Code, in different divisions, address a will made by a conservator. Paragraph (13) of section 2580(b) lists "Making a will" among the actions that may be proposed under the substituted judgment article. Section 6100, the general section on who may make a will, states in subdivision (a) that an individual 18 or more years of age who is of sound mind may make a will, and adds in subdivision (b) that a conservator may make a will for the conservatee if the conservator has been so authorized by a court order pursuant to section 2580. The same subdivision preserves the conservatee's own testamentary power: nothing in section 6100 impairs the right of a conservatee who is mentally competent to revoke or amend a will made by the conservator, or to make a new and inconsistent will. A will made by a conservator under such an order is therefore not the last word on the conservatee's testamentary dispositions if the conservatee is mentally competent. Whether any will has been or could be made for Marguerite A. Devlin under such an order is a question this sheet does not answer.

BENEFICIARY DESIGNATIONS, POLICY RIGHTS, AND A TRANSFER ON DEATH DEED (PROB. CODE § 2580(B)(8), (14))
Property that passes outside a will — life insurance, annuities, retirement and other employee benefit plans, and real property held under a revocable transfer on death deed — is reached by two paragraphs of the list. Paragraph (8) allows the proposed action to be the exercise of the conservatee's rights to elect benefit or payment options, to terminate, to change beneficiaries or ownership, to assign rights, to borrow, or to receive cash value in return for a surrender of rights, under life insurance policies, plans or benefits; annuity policies, plans or benefits; mutual fund and other dividend investment plans; and retirement, profit sharing and employee welfare plans and benefits. Paragraph (14) allows the proposed action to be the making or revoking of a revocable transfer on death deed. Both are among the actions that require a court order under this article; the statute lists them as things the conservator may petition to be authorized or required to do, not as things the conservator may do alone. Whether any such designation or deed exists in the estate of Marguerite A. Devlin is a question this sheet does not answer.

WHO MUST BE GIVEN NOTICE OF THE PETITION (PROB. CODE § 2581)
Section 2581 requires that notice of the hearing on a substituted judgment petition be given, regardless of age, for the period and in the manner provided in the Probate Code's general notice chapter, to five categories of persons: those entitled to notice under that general chapter; those required to be named in a petition for the appointment of a conservator; so far as is known to the petitioner, beneficiaries under any document executed by the conservatee which may have testamentary effect, unless the court for good cause dispenses with such notice; so far as is known to the petitioner, the persons who would be the conservatee's heirs under the laws of intestate succession if the conservatee were to die immediately, again unless the court for good cause dispenses with notice; and such other persons as the court may order. In Conservatorship of Hart the Court of Appeal declined to read the reference to beneficiaries as extending to unborn potential beneficiaries. Who would be entitled to notice in the conservatorship of Marguerite A. Devlin is a question this sheet does not answer.

THE TWO DETERMINATIONS THE COURT MUST MAKE (PROB. CODE § 2582)
Section 2582 states a condition on the court's power: the court "may make an order authorizing or requiring the proposed action under this article only if" it determines both of two things. The first concerns the conservatee's own position: the conservatee either is not opposed to the proposed action, or, if opposed to it, lacks legal capacity for the proposed action. A conservatee who is opposed and who has legal capacity for the action is therefore outside the section's terms. The second concerns the estate: either the proposed action will have no adverse effect on the estate, or the estate remaining after the action is taken will be adequate to provide for the needs of the conservatee and for the support of those legally entitled to support, maintenance and education from the conservatee, taking into account the age, physical condition, standards of living and all other relevant circumstances of the conservatee and of those persons. Whether either determination could be made in the conservatorship of Marguerite A. Devlin is a question this sheet does not answer.

Article 10 of Chapter 6 of Part 4 of Division 4 of the Probate Code, sections 2580 through 2586, is titled "Substituted Judgment." expectedJSON.body: Murphy v. Murphy concerned what a substituted judgment order settles once the conservatee has died. A probate court had authorized a conservator to execute a living trust and pour-over will that effectively disinherited one of the conservatee's children; after the conservatee's death that child sued his sister for breach of an oral testamentary contract, undue influence, interference with contract and fraud, and won a constructive trust over half the estate. The Court of Appeal reversed, holding as a matter of first impression that the action was barred by collateral estoppel. It concluded that the issues of fraud and undue influence had been adjudicated and necessarily decided in the substituted judgment proceeding, noting that the petition had expressly tendered those issues and that under section 2583 the probate court was required to consider all relevant circumstances and is presumed to have done so. The child had been given notice of that proceeding and could have objected there or appealed the order. Whether any order in the conservatorship of Marguerite A. Devlin would have preclusive effect in later litigation is a question this sheet does not answer.
